parsing_res_list.block_content: The Civil Commissioner in London announces that no further volunteers are required for mounted-ed Police
Mr. A. J. Cook and Mr. Frank Hodges will fly to Ostend to review to attend the International Miners' conference.
Further trouble occurred at Hull to-dry. The police charged the strikers with their batons in the City Square. Several were injured, seven being treated in the infirm.

Troops Not Called Up.
The War Office states that no troops have yet been called up to aid the civil power except as guards at vulnerable points.
Attention a full conference of the Christian Churches of Great

Britain, the Archbishop of Canterbury issued an appeal to all parties in the present crisis to resume negotiations, urging simultaneously and concurrently, firstly, that the Trade Union Congress cancel the general strike; secondly, that the Government renew its offer of assistance to the coal industry for a short period; and, thirdly, that the coal owners withdraw their new wares scale recently issued.
The British Worker appears half of yesterday's size. It declares that the Cabinet has stopped the supply of news print.

Three important London hospitals lack electricity owing to the Stepney power-station cutting off the supply: The British "Gazette" in this connection says that it shows the "incompetence of the Trade Union Congress, who promised that there would be no interference with the hospitals."
Numerous strikens have been sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour for interfering with the Police.
A Moscow report says that the Soviet General Council of Trade Unions has transferred two million roubles to the Trade Union Congress as a second instalment of the collection among the Soviet Unions.

No. Poulton. Publicity Chairman of the Trade Unions Congress states that the Council had heard nothing about the Red International financial assistance. It was impossible to say what would be the attitude of the Council if a gift were offered.

Failing to suppress the strikers' attempt to interfere with a volunteer bus in Cardiff the police charged with their truncheons. Some women were trampled in the stampede. Two persons were injured and one arrested.

The "British Gazette" contends that the fact that the "British Worker" is published entirely by Trade Unionists proves that the strike is purely political and aimed at the newspapers whose opinions the Trade Union Congress disapproves.
It states that apart from the miners the strikers do not exceed a million of whom vast numbers were ordered to strike without being consulted.
The issue has ceased to be industrial and has become political and constitutional.
The chief apostle of the labour general headquarters, Mr. Ernest Bevin, of the Transport and General Workers' Union, is the real commander-in-Chief of the general strike.
It is explained that the Danish sympathy strike cannot be fixed for a week and will not begin for a fortnight at the earliest.

The Trade Union Congress in an official statement states that local strike organisations have been authorised to meet employers and offer a supply of light and power for houses, streets, shops, and social services.
The statement emphasises that the Council does not challenge the Constitution and is not desirous of undermining Parliamentary institutions.
The Trade Union lenders have cancelled their continental engagement. Mr. Cook is not going to Ostend.

The General Federation of Trade
Unions has decided financially to
support the British戒icers as far
as possible by means of voluntary
contributions from workers in
Germany.
The Executive Committee of the Danish Trade Unions' to-day gave the Employers' Association preliminary notice of a strike in support of the British strikers.
Coal freights to the Mediterranean have been reduced fifteen per cent. Freights have slumped in spite of the rush, and a vast tonnage is available.
The price of bunker coal in the New Waterway for ships in bullast has risen to $24/ and for loaded ships $26/

The Secretary for the Colonies has, wirelessly brondeasted a message stating that members of the Colonial Service on leave can place their services at the disposal of the Government or local authorities as long as such arrangements do not interfere with their return to duty oversens.
In a riot at Glasgow there was injured a police sergeant who went to hospital suffering from head injuries and concussion. He was struck with a stone: A youth who dashed through a shattered window was seriously hurt.

Police baton charges were made
all duty long.
Further disturbances occurred in Edinburgh last night, the mob-stoning the Corporation bases. The Police charged the demonstrators and arrested nine.
There was rioting in Middlesbrough last night.

Official details show that heavy lorries were chained to rails in an attempt to wreck a late passenger train. A crowd prevented the closing of a level crossing, and the gates were invaded. A passenger station was wrecked and also a goods station. Serious damage was done.

In response to the Mayor's appeal Naval ratings cleared the line for traffic after several hours work.
The great trek to the City and westward on the fourth morning of the strike was most disagreeable, but there is no great diminution of the number of pedestrians using the attenuated service. Trains from many districts relieved the situation. Five hundred trains ran on the Southern Railway yesterday, as indicating the improvement in long-distance railway communications.
Twenty-two arrests were made, and it is stunted the disorders were entirely due to rowdies and not by strikers, who resent the disturbances.

to-day's "Yorkshire Post" was on sale in London at an early hour. The continental "Daily Mail" was distributed to London and Suburb. The most noteworthy development is the withdrawal by workers of the Union facilities for distribution of food and supplies from well-known caterers such as Lyons, but an army of volunteers are carrying on the distribution. At Edinburgh the Police, with batons drawn, repeatedly cleared the thoroughfares, but order was not restored until Mounted Police were called out. Many windows were smashed, including those of many business premises.

British Newspapers.
The Press situation continues to improve following the London papers publishing emergency editions to-day by the “Times,” “Daily Telegraph,” “Daily Express,” “Daily Mirror and “Daily Mail.”
Tram-cars and buses are running and the railway services are increased. OFFICIALS INDICTED.

The Federal Grand Jury have indicted Henry Daugherty, ex-Attorney-General, and Thomas Miller, ex-Allen Property Customer, for a conspiracy in connection with the disposal of the property of the American Metals Company.
The case involved property worth seven million dollars beize
during the war and belonging to enemy aliens.

The indictment is that it was part of the conspiracy to enable Daugherty, Miller, and others to receive from the claimants securities of $391,000 which were paid in for putting through the transfer deal.

The Rhenish-Westphalian Steel Trust officially exists to-day and is known as the Vereinigte Stahlwerke Ekiengesellschaft. It formally took over the Phoenix, Rheinstahl, Gelsenkirchen, Bochumverein, Deutsch-Luxemburg, Van Der Zypenwissen and Thyssen concerns. The managing director is Dr. Voegler. The capital is eight hundred million marks.

Further provincial newspapers are reappouring, and the Newspaper Society, in a statement, says the Provincial Press has vigorously replied to the attempt to muzzle it. Nearly every provincial newspaper from which information is received is publishing, and, in very many cases, editions and sizes are normal.
while the “Evening News” is publishing a special emergency edition this afternoon.
In several important centres it is reported that printing stuffs have refused to act unconstitutionally and have either remained at work or have returned after a brief absence.

Following the refusal of the Newport (Monmouth): Corporation to discontinue the supply of electrical power to industrial concerns, the strike committee have advised the withdrawal of men from the Power Station and operatives have been notified they must cease work this afternoon.
A further indication of railway improvement was shown in the special train bringing 550 liner passengers from Plymouth to London this afternoon.
The employees of the Newcastle Electric Supply Company struck last night, but the emergency staff are carrying on. Supply of power is uninterrupted.
A significant statement was made by the Speaker in the House of Commons, arising out of an enquiry whether arrangements will be made to enable the House to continue in session.

Notwithstanding the absence of a regular staff responsible for the ordinary services of the House, the Speaker said he regretted it was a fact that the men engaged on the staff of the principal services of the House had been withdrawn.
He assured the House he would not allow the House to be disabled.
If it became necessary he would conduct the House without any printing or electric light.
A Japanese View.
Tokyo, May 7.
The Ministry of Industry and Commerce, interviewing the Press, stated he did not think the British strikes was likely to cause Labour trouble in Japan, as the conditions

The League of Nations Health Committee has adopted the second part of the Medical Director's report on his voyage to the Far East relating to the work of the Singapore Epidemiological and Intelligence Bureau, and passed a number of resolutions concerning, interalia, the development of the League's epidemiological service and the establishment of close contact with the Japanese public health service activities.

The report pays a tribute to the notable services of the Bureau to Eastern health administration, especially in having kept them promptly informed in regard to a serious cholera outbreak in several Asiatic ports during the past twelve months.
Early 80-day the KIT will re- started following the failure of the peace parleys.
French airmen heavily bombed the Rif's positions.

No. 6, Cheung Hing Street, was put up for auction by Messrs. Hughes & Hough yesterday. The upset price was $10,000, with bids of $200 acceptable. Bidding rose to $11,600 when the property was knocked down to Mr. Ho Cheung-chee. The attendance was poor.
In spite of the strike the British delegation, headed by Lord Cecil, is leaving, for Geneva to-morrow, travelling by air to Paris to attend the meeting of the Committee on the composition of the Council of the League on Monday and thereafter the preliminary Disarmament Committee and the ordinary Council meeting in June at which Sir Austen Chamberlain will preside.
May 8—Queen's Theatre: Allaen Pringle & John Gilbert in His Hour
May 8—Star Theatre: "The Seventh Day" and the Moscow State Ballet.
May 8—World Theatre: Manors Daw in "Gambling Wives" May 17—Piano recital by the pupils of Mr. Harry Ore in the City Hall.

May 8—Annual athletic sports of the Victoria Recreation Club.
May 29—Opening Baseball match of this season between South China (champions) and Japanese Baseball Club.
